paragraphs: Friend, here's what I love about this passage: nobody in it is pretending to be fine. David says, "I am poor and needy," and the writer of Psalm 71 tells us his enemies are saying, "God has forsaken him" (Psalm 70:5; Psalm 71:11). Neither one cleans it up for company, and both keep praying anyway. Bring God the real, messy, no-apron-on version of you, because that's the only version He's asking to hear from.

Now watch what the writer does when the pressure is on. He says, "But I will always hope and will praise You more and more" (Psalm 71:14). He isn't praying his way OUT of his troubles first and praising later, and he says he'll declare God's righteousness and salvation even though he "cannot know their full measure" (Psalm 71:15). I think that's the whole trick: you don't need to understand all of God to lean on Him, you just need to keep leaning, like he has "since birth" (Psalm 71:6).

And then there's the part that gets me right in the mustache. He's old and gray, and his biggest prayer isn't comfort, it's "until I proclaim Your power to the next generation" (Psalm 71:18). Getting older doesn't end your usefulness to God, and somebody coming up behind you needs to hear what you've seen. So tell it, baker, and tell it LOUD, because God has "done great things" (Psalm 71:19).
